transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

I'm here because... well, I just can't shake this thought. I've been an electrician for years, you know? And if all that experience couldn't keep my own brother safe, then... I just feel like I'm a danger to anybody who works with me, or even lives under my roof.
You mentioned your brother—what happened to him, and do you believe you were directly responsible for it?

I honestly don't know exactly how to explain what happened. I just... I can't really go into the details of it right now. As for being directly responsible... I'm not sure. I just know I have all this experience, and it wasn't enough to protect him. That's... that's really all I know to say about it right now.

When you think about your brother's situation, do you believe that logically and factually you were responsible for what happened, or does it feel like you should have been able to prevent it even though you recognize that might not make complete sense?

I don't know about logically. I just... like I said earlier, I can't shake the thought that if all my years of experience as an electrician couldn't keep my own brother safe, then I'm just a danger to anybody who works with me. Or even anyone who lives under my roof. Factually or not, that's just how it is in my head.

When this thought comes to your mind—that you're a danger to people around you—does it feel like something your own mind is producing that you want to get rid of, or does it feel like a true reflection of who you are?

I mean... it's definitely my own thought. I don't hear voices or anything like that, if that's what you mean. But I don't really want to get rid of it, either, because... well, it feels true. It just feels like a fact. I didn't protect him, so I'm a risk to be around. It's just how I see myself now.
Over the past few weeks or months, have you noticed changes in your sleep, your appetite, or your energy levels?

My sleep has definitely changed. It's been pretty bad. Most nights I just lie there, wide awake, listening for... I don't know, crackling sounds or a car door in the driveway. And when I do finally manage to fall asleep, I jolt awake completely soaked through from dreams about the garage. 

Once that happens, I just can't get back down before I have to get up for work. So my energy is pretty shot during the day because of it. I haven't really paid much attention to my appetite, honestly, but the sleep is definitely a major problem right now.

Over the past few weeks, aside from these thoughts about being a danger to others, have you noticed that things that used to interest you or bring you pleasure—like hobbies, time with friends, or activities you enjoyed—just don't feel enjoyable anymore?

No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I still like doing the things I usually do. I still watch the games on the weekend, still like grabbing a beer with my buddies when I can. 

I might not do it quite as often right now just because I'm so beat from not sleeping, but... no, when I do go out or do my hobbies, I still enjoy them. I haven't really lost interest in that stuff.

When you wake up in the morning or think about your day ahead, how is your mood? Would you describe it as sad, empty, or hopeless, or is it more just anxious and worried about being a danger to others?

I wouldn't really say I feel sad or empty. And it's not exactly just being anxious, either. It's more like... there's this heavy mix of guilt and anger that just sits right in my chest all day long. 

It's hard to shake. It really hits me the hardest when I look at my nephew. I just look at him and think about how he lost his dad, and now he got stuck with me instead. So... yeah, that's mostly what my mood is like when I wake up and think about the day.

When you have this thought that you're a danger to people around you, do you find yourself doing things repeatedly to try to prevent harm—like checking electrical work multiple times, avoiding certain situations, or seeking reassurance from others that you won't hurt anyone?

I don't really do the checking things over and over. It's more that I just avoid things entirely. Like, I don't go in my own garage unless I absolutely have to. I actually quit helping with the electrical stuff at my church, too. 

And... if people bring things up, like if they start talking about car projects or the fire, I just shut them down fast. I just steer clear of all of it.

When you think about your brother's situation and feel like you're a danger to others—if I asked you to really think about it logically, do you actually believe that as an electrician you could have prevented what happened to him, or does some part of you know that wasn't realistic even though the guilt feeling won't go away?

I mean... I don't really know. I guess when people say it wasn't realistic for me to catch it, I hear the words, but... I just can't separate it out like that in my head. 

I'm an electrician. I work with this stuff every day. So even if part of me knows I wasn't there to inspect his house, the rest of me just thinks I should have known anyway. I don't really have a clear answer for you. The guilt just kind of overrides the logic, I guess.

When you have this thought that you're a danger to others—if you woke up tomorrow and that thought was completely gone, would you feel relieved and want it gone, or would you feel like something important about who you are had been taken away?

I don't really know. I've never thought about it like that. 

I mean, I guess I'd want to feel relieved. Nobody wants to walk around feeling like they're a threat to the people they care about. But... I can't even really picture waking up and just not having that thought anymore. It's so tied up in what happened with my brother. So, I'm not really sure how I'd actually feel if it was just suddenly gone. I don't really have a good answer for you on that one.

When you have this thought that you're a danger to others—does it feel like a natural part of how you see yourself and what you deserve, or does it feel like a thought that's being forced into your mind against your will, even though you can't get rid of it?

It doesn't feel forced into my mind, like... like someone else put it there. It just feels like a fact. Like it's just the truth of who I am now. 

I mean, considering what happened, it feels natural that I'd think that way. It's just how I see myself. I don't feel like I'm fighting off some weird thought that doesn't belong to me. It's just... it's just what I believe about myself now.

If someone you trusted completely told you that you were not actually responsible for what happened to your brother, and that your guilt wasn't justified—would you be able to accept that, or would you still feel deep down that you deserved to feel guilty regardless of what they said?

I think I'd still feel deep down that I deserved it. People I trust have actually tried telling me it wasn't my fault, but... it just doesn't change anything. 

That's honestly why I came in here to begin with. I just can't shake the thought that if all my years as an electrician couldn't keep my own brother safe, then I'm a danger to anybody who works with me, or even anyone who lives under my roof. No matter what someone else tells me, that's just what I'm left with.

opening_question.question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: Patient presents with persistent intrusive thoughts of guilt and self-blame following brother's death, accompanied by sleep disturbance, hypervigilance (listening for sounds), nightmares about the incident, avoidance behaviors, and functional impairment. While guilt-ridden cognitions are present, they are ego-syntonic (feel like facts/truth about self) rather than ego-dystonic obsessions. The clinical picture is consistent with Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder with prominent guilt-based rumination and avoidance, rather than OCD or Major Depressive Disorder, as mood is characterized by guilt/anger rather than sadness/emptiness, and anhedonia is absent.

confirmed_symptoms: Hypervigilance (listening for crackling sounds, car doors)
Intrusive guilt-based thoughts about responsibility and being a danger
Quit helping with electrical work at church
Steers clear of conversations about car projects or the fire
Avoids situations related to the incident
Unable to return to sleep after nightmares
Reduced daytime energy due to sleep deprivation
Self-blame and sense of deserved guilt
Belief that he is a danger to others around him
Guilt intensified when seeing nephew (brother's son)

diagnostic_checklist.duration_verified: Symptoms present for 'past few weeks or months' with ongoing persistence; brother's death appears to be recent traumatic event triggering PTSD presentation
additional_requirements: Qualifying traumatic event: Brother's death (electrician-related incident in garage/car fire)
Intrusive guilt-based cognitions tied to traumatic event
Avoidance of trauma-related cues and situations
Functional impairment: reduced work involvement, social withdrawal, changed relationships
Guilt is ego-syntonic (feels like truth about self) rather than ego-dystonic, distinguishing from OCD
Anhedonia absent; patient retains interest in hobbies and social activities when energy permits
